en.title: Education Mathematics: the whole course
en.short: What education mathematics covers, how the degree is organised, the main areas and how to study it.

sections.heading: What the subject is
sections.text:
Education mathematics is the study of mathematics and of how to teach it. It prepares teachers of mathematics for schools, colleges and other learning settings. About half of the work is the subject itself: number, algebra, geometry, trigonometry, calculus, probability, statistics, analysis, abstract algebra and modelling. The other half is education: how learners think, how curricula are built, how lessons are planned, how assessment works, how to include all learners, and how teachers grow professionally.

The field asks what mathematics is, why it is taught, how understanding develops, and how teaching can be improved. Graduates may teach, write learning materials, assess learning, support curriculum work or carry out research. Good teachers need both strong mathematics and a clear understanding of learners.

sections.heading: How the degree is usually organised
sections.text:
Length and awards differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook. In Nigeria, universities commonly award B.Ed or B.Sc.(Ed) after about four years for entry by UTME, with teaching practice and a final project. Direct entry can shorten the route. Colleges of education award the NCE, commonly a three-year route, and some graduates continue to degrees. In Ghana and South Africa, a B.Ed is also a common route and commonly takes four years, but entry rules and accreditation differ. Some countries use a first degree in mathematics followed by a teaching qualification.

Programmes usually mix campus courses, micro-teaching, school observation, teaching practice and a project. The education courses and the mathematics courses support each other. Do not treat one half as optional.

sections.heading: Main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
The introductory stage starts with the nature and aims of mathematics education, sets, logic and number systems, algebra and functions, geometry and trigonometry, calculus foundations, and probability and statistics foundations. It then adds learning theories for mathematics, the mathematics curriculum and syllabus, and lesson planning and classroom communication.

The core stage has two strands. The mathematics strand covers linear algebra and matrices, real analysis and advanced calculus, and abstract algebra and number theory. The education strand covers methods of teaching mathematics, assessment and evaluation, problem solving and proof, and subject-specific methods for number and algebra, geometry and measurement, calculus and analysis, and statistics and probability. It continues with mathematical modelling and applications, educational technology, inclusive and differentiated mathematics, language and communication, teacher professionalism and ethics, teaching practice and reflection, and research methods.

At master’s level, students study advanced theories of mathematics learning, mathematics teacher knowledge and development, curriculum policy and reform, and advanced research in mathematics education.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Study mathematics actively. Work examples without looking at the solution, then check. Keep an error log and revisit weak topics. For proof and problem solving, write the reason for each step. Use the school syllabus alongside your own mathematics so you see how advanced ideas appear in simpler form.

For education courses, turn theory into classroom decisions. Ask what you would do, why, and what evidence would show learning. Practise explaining a topic aloud in simple language. Plan short lessons with a clear goal, an example, a task and a check. Observe teachers and record what worked. After teaching practice, write briefly about what you would change.

Use official curriculum and assessment documents for your country, and check them because they change. Read research carefully: a small study supports only limited claims.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
Students often treat education courses as easy talk and mathematics as the only real work. Both are wrong. You need deep mathematics and knowledge of how learners learn it. Another common fault is memorising a proof without understanding why each step follows.

In lesson planning, many students list activities but do not state the mathematical goal or how learning will be checked. Some teach by talking only, without tasks, questions or feedback. Others ignore learners’ misconceptions, or assume that a correct answer proves understanding.

In assessment, a common mistake is testing only recall. In professional studies, students sometimes present one country’s curriculum, assessment or teacher registration rules as universal. Always name the country and check the current official source. In research, do not make broad claims from a small sample or from content analysis alone.

keyPoints: Education mathematics joins deep subject knowledge with knowledge of how learners learn mathematics.
Degrees and awards differ by country and institution, so check your handbook and official regulator.
The course moves from foundations to core mathematics, teaching methods, professional studies and research.
Learn mathematics by solving and proving, and learn teaching by planning, explaining, assessing and reflecting.
A lesson plan needs a clear mathematical goal, not only activities.
Name the country whenever you discuss curriculum, assessment or teacher registration rules.

en.title: Nature and Aims of Mathematics Education
en.short: What mathematics is, aims and literacy, the teacher’s role, and doing versus teaching mathematics.

sections.heading: Mathematics as discipline
sections.text: Mathematics is the study of patterns, quantity, space, structure and change. As a discipline, it builds definitions, axioms (starting assumptions), proofs and models, and it grows by asking new questions. As a school subject, it is a selection from the discipline, arranged for learners and taught with methods, examples and assessment. The two are related but not identical: school mathematics is chosen, simplified and sequenced.

sections.heading: Aims and literacy
sections.text: Aims state what mathematics education is for. Common aims include numeracy (using number and measurement), problem solving, reasoning, communication, a positive attitude, preparation for work and further study, and informed citizenship. Mathematical literacy is the ability to use mathematics to understand and act in real situations; definitions vary between countries and international surveys. Aims are not universal. They change with policy, culture and economy, so check the current national curriculum, ministry guidelines and examination syllabus for your country.

sections.heading: Doing and teaching
sections.text: Doing mathematics means solving a problem yourself. Teaching mathematics means designing conditions so that others can learn it. A teacher must know the mathematics, anticipate errors, choose examples and diagrams, explain why rules work, use language clearly and assess understanding. For example, a teacher in Kano, Amina, can solve 3x + 5 = 20 herself. Teaching it requires asking what x means, why subtract 5 first, and how to check x = 5. She plans questions and support, not only the answer.

sections.heading: Teacher’s role
sections.text: The teacher connects the subject, the learner and the curriculum. This includes planning, setting tasks, giving feedback, managing the classroom, supporting language, and building confidence. The role is professional, not merely technical: teachers adapt policy to learners and report honestly on progress. Because aims and policy vary by country and over time, always check official documents rather than assuming one system’s rules apply everywhere.

keyPoints: Mathematics as a discipline studies patterns, quantity, space, structure and change; school mathematics is a selected and sequenced version.
Aims of mathematics education commonly include numeracy, problem solving, reasoning, communication, positive attitudes, preparation and citizenship.
Mathematical literacy means using mathematics to understand and act in real situations, and its definition varies.
Doing mathematics is solving a problem; teaching mathematics is designing conditions and support so others learn it.
The teacher plans, explains, assesses, supports language and builds confidence, and adapts policy to learners.
Aims and policy differ by country and change over time; check current official curriculum and examination documents.

en.title: Sets, Logic and Number Systems
en.short: Set operations, truth tables and the natural, integer, rational and real number systems.

sections.heading: Sets and operations
sections.text:
A set is a collection of elements. x ∈ A means x is in A; A ⊆ B means every element of A is in B. The empty set is ∅. A ∪ B contains elements in A or B; A ∩ B contains elements in both; A \ B contains elements in A but not B; A′ is the complement (elements of the universal set not in A).

Example: A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {2, 3, 4} give A ∪ B = {1, 2, 3, 4}, A ∩ B = {2, 3}, and A \ B = {1}.

sections.heading: Logic and truth tables
sections.text:
A statement is either true or false. ¬P reverses the truth value. P ∧ Q is true only when both are true. P ∨ Q is true when at least one is true. P → Q is false only when P is true and Q is false. P ↔ Q is true when P and Q have the same truth value.

A truth table lists all combinations; two statements give 2² = 4 rows. For example, true P and false Q make P → Q false but P ∨ Q true.

sections.heading: Number systems and properties
sections.text:
The natural numbers N are the counting numbers, often {1, 2, 3, ...}; some texts include 0. The integers Z add zero and negatives: {..., −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, ...}. A rational number is a fraction a/b where a and b are integers and b ≠ 0. The real numbers R include all rationals and all irrationals, such as √2.

The systems differ in closure. N is closed under + and ×, not − or ÷. Z is closed under +, −, ×, not ÷. Q and R are closed under +, −, ×, ÷, except ÷ by 0. Addition and multiplication are commutative and associative, and multiplication distributes over addition: a × (b + c) = (a × b) + (a × c). An identity leaves a number unchanged: 0 for addition, 1 for multiplication. An inverse combines with a number to give the identity: −a for addition, 1/a for multiplication (a ≠ 0).

keyPoints: A set is a collection of elements; x ∈ A means x is in A, and A ⊆ B means every element of A is in B.
A ∪ B contains elements in A or B; A ∩ B contains elements in both; A \ B contains elements in A but not B.
P ∧ Q is true only when both are true; P → Q is false only when P is true and Q is false.
A truth table with n statements has 2ⁿ rows.
N = {1, 2, 3, ...} (some texts include 0); Z adds zero and negatives; Q = {a/b : a, b ∈ Z, b ≠ 0}; R includes rationals and irrationals.
Closure, commutativity, associativity, distributivity, identity and inverses describe number systems; a × (b + c) = (a × b) + (a × c).

en.title: Algebra and Functions for Teaching
en.short: Expressions, equations, inequalities, polynomials, indices, logarithms, functions and graph transformations.

sections.heading: Expressions and equations
sections.text: An algebraic expression combines numbers, variables and operations, such as 3x²−5x+2. A polynomial is an expression whose terms have non-negative integer powers; its degree is the highest power, so this example has degree 2. An equation states that two expressions are equal. Solve 2x+3=11 by subtracting 3: 2x=8, then dividing by 2: x=4. Check: 2(4)+3=11. An inequality compares expressions. Solve −2x<6 by dividing by −2 and reversing the sign: x>−3. Check x=0: 0<6 is true. Common errors include dropping the sign reversal and treating (x+3)² as x²+9; it is x²+6x+9.

sections.heading: Indices and logarithms
sections.text: Indices are powers. The laws a^m×a^n=a^(m+n) and (a^m)^n=a^(mn) follow from repeated multiplication. A logarithm answers a power question: log_b x is the exponent to which base b must be raised to give x, with b>0, b≠1 and x>0. So log_2 8=3 because 2³=8. The product law is log_b(xy)=log_b x+log_b y. It does not apply to sums: log_2(4+4)=log_2 8=3, while log_2 4+log_2 4=2+2=4. Common errors are using log(a+b)=log a+log b and forgetting that log_b 1=0 and log_b b=1.

sections.heading: Functions and graphs
sections.text: A function assigns exactly one output to each allowed input. The set of allowed inputs is the domain; the set of outputs is the range. For f(x)=x², the domain is all real numbers and the range is y≥0. A graph shows all input-output pairs. Transformations change the graph: y=f(x−2)+3 moves y=f(x) right by 2 and up by 3. y=−f(x) reflects it in the x-axis. Common errors are shifting f(x−2) left instead of right, and reading a graph without checking its scale.

sections.heading: Teaching connections
sections.text: School algebra stresses procedures; first-year study asks why they work and adds formal language such as domain, range and function notation. A teacher should connect tables, graphs, words and symbols, and use substitution to check answers. Anticipate the errors above, ask pupils to explain each step, and choose examples that expose misconceptions. In a teacher-education degree, this subject knowledge supports later work on methods, assessment and lesson planning, which are covered elsewhere.

keyPoints: An expression has no equals sign; an equation states equality and an inequality compares expressions.
Solve equations by inverse operations and check by substitution; when multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number, reverse the sign.
A polynomial has non-negative integer powers; its degree is the highest power.
Indices follow a^m×a^n=a^(m+n) and (a^m)^n=a^(mn); log_b x is the exponent that gives x, and log_b(xy)=log_b x+log_b y.
A function gives one output for each allowed input; domain is the set of inputs and range the set of outputs.
For y=f(x), f(x−2)+3 shifts the graph right 2 and up 3; common errors include (x+3)²≠x²+9 and log(a+b)≠log a+log b.

en.title: Geometry and Trigonometry
en.short: Euclidean geometry, angles, triangles, circles, coordinates, trigonometric ratios and rules.

sections.heading: Points, lines and angles
sections.text: Euclidean geometry studies points, lines, planes and shapes built from them, using definitions, axioms and deductive reasoning. A point has position but no size; a line extends without end; a plane is a flat surface. An angle is formed by two rays from a common point, measured in degrees (°). A right angle is 90°, a straight angle is 180°, and angles on a straight line add to 180°. Vertically opposite angles are equal. When a transversal cuts parallel lines, corresponding angles are equal and alternate angles are equal. Draw with a ruler, protractor and compass; measure to check. The interior angles of any triangle add to 180°.

sections.heading: Triangles, circles, coordinates
sections.text: Triangles are classified by sides (equilateral, isosceles, scalene) and angles (acute, right, obtuse). Congruent triangles are identical in shape and size. A circle is the set of points at a fixed distance (radius) from a centre; diameter = 2 × radius. A chord joins two points on a circle; a tangent touches it at one point. In coordinate geometry, a point is (x, y) on axes. Distance between (x1, y1) and (x2, y2) is √((x2 − x1)² + (y2 − y1)²); midpoint is ((x1 + x2) ÷ 2, (y1 + y2) ÷ 2); gradient = (y2 − y1) ÷ (x2 − x1).

sections.heading: Trigonometric ratios and rules
sections.text: In a right-angled triangle, for angle θ: sin θ = opposite ÷ hypotenuse, cos θ = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse, tan θ = opposite ÷ adjacent. Use these to find a side or angle. The identity sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 follows from Pythagoras, and tan θ = sin θ ÷ cos θ. For non-right triangles use the sine rule a ÷ sin A = b ÷ sin B = c ÷ sin C and the cosine rule a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A. Applications include heights, distances and bearings. Worked example: in triangle ABC, A = 40°, B = 60°, a = 8 cm. Then b = a sin B ÷ sin A = 8 × 0.8660 ÷ 0.6428 ≈ 10.8 cm. Construct the triangle with ruler and protractor and measure b; it should be near 10.8 cm.

keyPoints: The interior angles of a triangle add to 180°.
For a right triangle, sin θ = opposite ÷ hypotenuse, cos θ = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse and tan θ = opposite ÷ adjacent.
The sine rule is a ÷ sin A = b ÷ sin B = c ÷ sin C.
The cosine rule is a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A.
The identity sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 holds for all angles θ.
Drawing and measuring a figure is a useful check on a calculation.

en.title: Calculus Foundations
en.short: Limits, continuity, differentiation, integration and simple applications for first-year students.

sections.heading: Limits and continuity
sections.text: A limit is the value a function approaches as its input approaches a point. We write lim as x tends to a of f(x) = L. The idea is intuitive: choose x close to a, and f(x) becomes close to L. A function is continuous at a if its limit there equals its value, f(a). Roughly, the graph has no break or jump at that point. For example, f(x) = x² is continuous at x = 3 because as x approaches 3, x² approaches 9, and f(3) = 9. First-year work uses these ideas to prepare for formal analysis later.

sections.heading: Differentiation
sections.text: Differentiation finds the derivative, the instantaneous rate of change or slope of the tangent. For powers, if y = x^n then dy/dx = n x^(n−1). Constants multiply, and sums differentiate term by term. Also sin x gives cos x, cos x gives −sin x, e^x gives e^x, and ln x gives 1/x. Example: y = 3x² + 2x, so dy/dx = 6x + 2. At x = 2 the slope is 6×2 + 2 = 14. A positive derivative means the function is rising there; a negative one means it is falling.

sections.heading: Integration and applications
sections.text: Integration reverses differentiation. An indefinite integral includes a constant C. A definite integral gives signed area between the curve and the x-axis. For powers, ∫x^n dx = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + C, n ≠ −1. Also ∫sin x dx = −cos x + C, ∫e^x dx = e^x + C, and ∫1/x dx = ln|x| + C. Example: ∫ from 0 to 2 of 3x² dx = [x³] from 0 to 2 = 8 − 0 = 8. Applications: if s(t) is distance, ds/dt is speed; integrating a rate gives total change. For optimisation, set dy/dx = 0, then use the second derivative: positive gives a minimum, negative a maximum. When you teach this, everyday examples such as speed on a journey make rate of change concrete.

sections.heading: Common errors
sections.text: Common errors include dropping +C in indefinite integrals, forgetting to divide by n+1, and treating dy/dx as a fraction without care. In applied problems, state units and check that an answer is sensible. A derivative of a polynomial lowers the degree by one; an integral raises it by one. Always test an optimisation answer against the situation, not only the algebra. As a future teacher, expect your pupils to make these same mistakes, and plan your lessons to address them.

keyPoints: A limit describes the value a function approaches; continuity means the limit equals the function value.
The derivative dy/dx gives instantaneous rate of change; the power rule is y = x^n gives dy/dx = n x^(n−1).
Standard derivatives include sin x gives cos x, cos x gives −sin x, e^x gives e^x, and ln x gives 1/x.
Integration reverses differentiation; ∫x^n dx = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + C for n ≠ −1.
A definite integral gives signed area; ∫ from 0 to 2 of 3x² dx = 8.
For optimisation set dy/dx = 0 and use the second derivative to classify the point.

en.title: Probability and Statistics Foundations
en.short: Data presentation, centre and spread, probability rules, conditional probability, distributions and reading claims.

sections.heading: Data and graphs
sections.text:
Data come from surveys, experiments or observation. A variable is qualitative (categories) or quantitative (numbers, discrete or continuous). Use a frequency table, then a bar chart for categories, a histogram for grouped numbers, or a line graph for time.

Check axes, units, scale and sample size. A truncated axis can exaggerate change, and a biased sample cannot support a claim about a population.

sections.heading: Centre and spread
sections.text:
Centre: mean = Σx ÷ n; median = middle value after ordering; mode = most frequent. Spread: range = largest − smallest; variance = mean of squared deviations; standard deviation = √variance.

For 2, 4, 4, 6, 9:
n = 5, Σx = 25, mean = 5, median = 4, mode = 4, range = 7.
Squared deviations sum to 28.
Population variance = 28 ÷ 5 = 5.6, standard deviation ≈ 2.37.
Sample variance = 28 ÷ 4 = 7, standard deviation ≈ 2.65.

sections.heading: Probability rules
sections.text:
Probability is a number from 0 to 1. The sample space is all outcomes. For equally likely outcomes, P(A) = favourable ÷ total. P(not A) = 1 − P(A). P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B). For independent events (one does not change the other’s probability), P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B). Conditional probability P(A|B) = P(A and B) ÷ P(B).

With a fair die, P(even or more than 3) = 3/6 + 3/6 − 2/6 = 4/6 = 2/3. P(even | more than 3) = (2/6) ÷ (3/6) = 2/3.

sections.heading: Distributions and claims
sections.text:
Common distributions: binomial for a fixed number of independent trials with two outcomes, P(X = k) = C(n,k) p^k (1 − p)^(n−k), where C(n,k) is the number of combinations and p is the success probability; normal for many symmetric continuous variables, described by mean μ and standard deviation σ.

Interpret claims cautiously: correlation is not causation, a small or biased sample is weak evidence, and a headline may omit uncertainty. Check the source and the method before accepting a statistical claim.

keyPoints: Data may be qualitative or quantitative; present them with suitable tables and graphs, and check axes, scale and sample bias.
Mean = Σx ÷ n; median is the middle ordered value; mode is the most frequent value.
Range = largest − smallest; variance is the mean squared deviation; standard deviation = √variance.
P(not A) = 1 − P(A); P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B); for independent events P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).
Conditional probability P(A|B) = P(A and B) ÷ P(B).
Binomial P(X = k) = C(n,k) p^k (1 − p)^(n−k); normal data are described by mean μ and standard deviation σ; correlation is not causation.

en.title: Learning Theories for Mathematics
en.short: Behaviourist, cognitivist, constructivist and social learning theories, and what each means for teaching mathematics.

sections.heading: Four families of theory
sections.text:
Behaviourism sees learning as a change in observable behaviour caused by stimuli and consequences. Skinner’s operant conditioning uses reinforcement: a correct answer followed by praise is more likely to recur. In mathematics this supports clear steps, worked examples, immediate feedback and practice, but it does not explain understanding.

Cognitivism treats learning as information processing. New ideas enter working memory, which is limited, and are organised into schemas (mental frameworks) in long-term memory. Cognitive load theory says avoid unnecessary detail and chunk steps. Ausubel’s meaningful learning links new work to what students already know.

Constructivism holds that learners build knowledge by adjusting schemas through assimilation (fitting new ideas into existing schemas) and accommodation (changing a schema when it does not fit). Piaget described disequilibrium when old ideas fail. Vygotsky’s social constructivism adds the zone of proximal development (what a learner can do with help but not yet alone) and scaffolding. Social learning theory (Bandura) stresses observation, modelling and self-efficacy.

sections.heading: Memory, motivation, transfer
sections.text: Working memory holds only a few items, so break long procedures into chunks and use spaced retrieval. Motivation can be intrinsic (interest, competence) or extrinsic (marks, praise). Bandura’s self-efficacy, belief in one’s ability, predicts persistence; small successes build it. Transfer is using learning in a new context. Near transfer stays similar; far transfer is harder. Vary examples and ask students to compare, so they see structure, not surface.

sections.heading: Misconceptions and a case
sections.text: Common misconceptions include 'multiplication always makes bigger' and 'division always makes smaller', which fail with fractions; and reading 2a as '2 apples’ rather than 2 × a. A teacher in Kano, Mrs Adeyemi, asks pupils to test 1/2 × 3. Since 1/2 × 3 = 1.5, the answer is smaller than 3, so the rule is false. She then models the area model and gives guided practice. This combines constructivist conflict with behaviourist feedback and social modelling.

keyPoints: Behaviourism uses reinforcement, clear steps and immediate feedback to shape mathematical behaviour.
Cognitivism explains that working memory is limited and schemas organise long-term knowledge.
Constructivism says learners build new ideas from prior knowledge, often through conflict and scaffolding.
Social learning theory adds modelling, observation and self-efficacy.
Transfer improves when examples vary and students compare underlying structure.
Misconceptions need testing, cognitive conflict and corrective feedback, not only more practice.

en.title: Mathematics Curriculum and Syllabus
en.short: Curriculum models, syllabus structure and sequencing, schemes of work, and official documents.

sections.heading: Curriculum and aims
sections.text: A curriculum is the whole plan of what is taught, why, how and how it is assessed. Models include subject-centred, which stresses mathematical content and skills; learner-centred, which starts from learners’ needs and interests; outcomes-based, which states what learners should be able to do; and competence-based, which emphasises applying knowledge. Aims guide selection: common aims include numeracy, problem solving, reasoning, communication and positive attitudes, but official aims differ by country.

sections.heading: Syllabus structure
sections.text: A syllabus is the subject plan: topics, learning objectives, content, suggested activities, resources and assessment. Mathematics syllabuses are often organised by strands such as number, algebra, geometry and statistics, then sequenced by level. Prerequisites come first, and topics are revisited in a spiral. For example, Nigeria’s NERDC curriculum documents and WAEC or NECO examination syllabuses show this, as do England’s National Curriculum programmes of study. Examination syllabuses also state assessment objectives and paper structure. Always check the current official version.

sections.heading: Schemes of work
sections.text: A scheme of work turns the syllabus into a term or year plan: week, topic, objectives, activities, resources, assessment and time. It should be realistic and flexible. Example: a 12-week term with 3 mathematics periods a week gives 36 periods. A teacher might allocate 8 to number, 8 to algebra, 8 to geometry, 6 to statistics and 6 to revision and assessment; 8+8+8+6+6=36. Adjust after checking the school calendar.

sections.heading: Documents and change
sections.text: National curriculum and examination documents are official references, but they differ between countries and are revised. Use the latest version from the ministry, curriculum council or examination board. The syllabus is the official subject outline; the scheme of work is the teacher’s working plan. Good schemes link aims, sequence and assessment without copying the syllabus word for word.

keyPoints: A curriculum is the overall plan; a syllabus is the subject outline; a scheme of work is the teacher’s term or year plan.
Curriculum models include subject-centred, learner-centred, outcomes-based and competence-based, and each shapes aims differently.
Mathematics syllabuses usually group content into strands and sequence topics from prerequisites to later work, often revisiting ideas in a spiral.
A scheme of work should state week, topic, objectives, activities, resources, assessment and time.
Official curriculum and examination documents differ by country and are revised, so check the current version.
In a 12-week term with 3 periods a week, there are 36 periods to allocate.

en.title: Lesson Planning and Classroom Communication
en.short: Learning objectives, schemes of work, lesson plans, explanation, questioning, board work and group talk.

sections.heading: Objectives and schemes
sections.text:
A learning objective states what students should know or be able to do by the end of a lesson. Use an observable verb, such as solve, draw, explain or calculate, and add the condition where useful (for example, 'given a word problem'). For example: 'By the end of the lesson, students will be able to solve two-step linear equations and check their answers.' Success criteria are short statements that help students judge whether they have met the objective.

A scheme of work is a longer plan, usually for a term or year. It lists topics in order, with objectives, activities, resources and assessment, and should match the official syllabus. Formats vary by school and country.

sections.heading: Lesson plan format
sections.text:
Most lesson plans record the class, date, topic, prior knowledge, objectives, resources and timing. A common structure is starter, main activities and plenary. The starter recalls needed ideas. The main part models a skill, then gives guided and independent practice. The plenary reviews the objective and checks learning.

Include key questions and assessment. Keep timings realistic. A plan is a guide, not a script.

sections.heading: Explanation and questioning
sections.text: Explanation should be clear and step by step. Link new ideas to prior knowledge, give one worked example, and pause for questions. Avoid overload: one idea at a time. Questioning checks understanding. Plan key questions, use wait time (a pause of a few seconds before taking answers), and invite several students to answer. Closed questions test facts; open questions ask for reasoning, such as 'Why does this step work?'

sections.heading: Board work and routines
sections.text:
Board work should be organised: write the date and topic, keep a clear space for examples, write legibly, and do not block the board while talking. Work through examples line by line.

Group talk needs a clear task, roles and ground rules. Monitor and intervene. Basic routines cover entry, seating, materials, an attention signal, transitions and exit. For example, Mrs Adeyemi writes her objective, starts with a short recall task, models one example, then gives pairs a question to discuss before a whole-class plenary.

keyPoints: A learning objective states what students can do by the end, using an observable verb.
A scheme of work sequences topics for a term or year; a lesson plan details one lesson.
A common lesson plan has starter, main activities and plenary, with timing and assessment.
Explanation should be step by step and linked to prior knowledge.
Questioning, board work and group talk should be planned and monitored.
Basic routines make transitions calm and protect learning time.

en.title: Linear Algebra and Matrices
en.short: Vectors, matrices, determinants, systems, linear transformations and eigenvalues, with teaching links.

sections.heading: Core objects
sections.text: A vector is an ordered list of numbers; in school work it is often an arrow with size and direction. A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers. An m × n matrix has m rows and n columns. Matrices add entry by entry and multiply when the first matrix’s column count equals the second’s row count. For A = [[a,b],[c,d]], det A = ad − bc. If det A ≠ 0, A has an inverse.

sections.heading: Solving systems
sections.text: A system of linear equations can be written Ax = b. Gaussian elimination uses row operations to reduce it to a simpler form. If det A ≠ 0, there is one solution, x = A⁻¹b. Example: solve 2x + y = 5 and x − y = 1. Adding gives 3x = 6, so x = 2; then y = 1. Check: 2(2)+1=5 and 2−1=1. The coefficient matrix has det = 2(−1) − 1(1) = −3, so the solution is unique.

sections.heading: Transformations and eigenvalues
sections.text: A linear transformation maps vectors so that T(u+v)=T(u)+T(v) and T(cu)=cT(u). In finite dimensions it can be represented by a matrix: T(x)=Ax. An eigenvalue λ satisfies Av=λv for some nonzero vector v, called an eigenvector. Find eigenvalues from det(A−λI)=0, where I is the identity matrix. For A=[[2,1],[1,2]], det(A−λI)=(2−λ)²−1=λ²−4λ+3, so λ=3 or λ=1. Eigenvalues describe stretching directions and appear in vibration, population and data problems.

sections.heading: Curriculum and teaching
sections.text: Linear algebra connects school vectors and matrices to university mathematics. In school, vectors support geometry and mechanics; matrices model transformations and data tables. At university, linear algebra underpins calculus of several variables, differential equations, statistics and computer science. For a teacher, subject knowledge must be paired with clear representations: arrows for vectors, grids for matrices, and small numerical examples. Applications include computer graphics, economics, engineering and data analysis. Check your national syllabus for where each idea appears.

keyPoints: A vector is an ordered list; a matrix is a rectangular array, and an m × n matrix has m rows and n columns.
For A = [[a,b],[c,d]], det A = ad − bc; A is invertible exactly when det A ≠ 0.
A system Ax = b has a unique solution x = A⁻¹b when det A ≠ 0; Gaussian elimination solves it by row operations.
A linear transformation satisfies T(u+v)=T(u)+T(v) and T(cu)=cT(u), and in finite dimensions T(x)=Ax.
Eigenvalues satisfy Av=λv and det(A−λI)=0; eigenvectors are the nonzero vectors v.
Linear algebra links school vectors and matrices to university mathematics and applications such as graphics, data and engineering.

en.title: Real Analysis and Advanced Calculus
en.short: Sequences, series, limits, continuity, differentiation and integration with proofs and convergence theorems.

sections.heading: Limits and sequences
sections.text: Real analysis makes calculus precise. A sequence (a_n) converges to L if, for every ε > 0, there is N such that |a_n − L| < ε for n > N. This ε-N definition is the model for later proofs. A function tends to L at c if its values can be made close to L by taking x close to c, but not equal to c. Proofs use inequalities, including the triangle inequality |x + y| ≤ |x| + |y|.

sections.heading: Series and convergence
sections.text: A series Σ a_n converges when its partial sums s_n = a_1 + ... + a_n have a limit. The geometric series Σ r^n from n=1 to infinity converges to r/(1−r) when |r| < 1. For r = 3/4, the sum is (3/4)/(1 − 3/4) = 3. Tests include comparison, ratio, root and alternating series. Absolute convergence implies convergence, but not the reverse.

sections.heading: Continuity and differentiation
sections.text: A function f is continuous at c when lim x→c f(x) = f(c). In ε-δ form, for every ε > 0 there is δ > 0 such that |f(x) − f(c)| < ε whenever |x − c| < δ. Differentiability is stronger: f'(c) = lim h→0 (f(c+h) − f(c))/h. Differentiability implies continuity, but continuity does not imply differentiability; f(x)=|x| is continuous at 0 and not differentiable there. The mean value theorem links a function to its derivative.

sections.heading: Integration and theorems
sections.text: The Riemann integral is a limit of sums over partitions. Continuous functions on a closed interval are integrable. The fundamental theorem of calculus connects integration and differentiation: if f is continuous and F(x)=∫_a^x f(t)dt, then F'(x)=f(x), and ∫_a^b f(x)dx = F(b) − F(a) for an antiderivative F. Uniform convergence preserves continuity and permits term-by-term operations under stated conditions. These results are proved from definitions.

keyPoints: Convergence of a sequence means |a_n − L| < ε for all n > N, given any ε > 0.
A series converges when its partial sums converge; Σ r^n from n=1 equals r/(1−r) for |r| < 1.
Absolute convergence implies convergence, but convergence does not imply absolute convergence.
Differentiability implies continuity, but continuity does not imply differentiability.
If f is continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b), the mean value theorem gives f'(c) = (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a) for some c in (a,b).
The fundamental theorem gives F'(x)=f(x) for F(x)=∫_a^x f(t)dt and ∫_a^b f = F(b) − F(a).

en.title: Abstract Algebra and Number Theory
en.short: Groups, rings, fields, divisibility, primes, modular arithmetic and proof for teaching.

sections.heading: Groups, rings, fields
sections.text: A group is a set with one operation that is associative, has an identity element, and gives every element an inverse. The integers under addition form a group. A ring has two operations: addition forms a commutative group, multiplication is associative, and multiplication distributes over addition. The integers form a ring but not a field. A field is a commutative ring in which every nonzero element has a multiplicative inverse. The rational numbers form a field; the integers do not, because 2 has no integer inverse. These structures appear in school arithmetic, fractions and clock numbers.

sections.heading: Divisibility and primes
sections.text: An integer a divides b if b = ak for some integer k. A prime is an integer greater than 1 whose only positive divisors are 1 and itself. The fundamental theorem of arithmetic says every integer greater than 1 factors uniquely into primes, apart from order. For 84 and 30: 84 = 2² × 3 × 7 and 30 = 2 × 3 × 5, so gcd(84, 30) = 6 and lcm(84, 30) = 2² × 3 × 5 × 7 = 420. Check: 6 × 420 = 2,520 = 84 × 30. Prime factorisation explains divisibility tests and fraction simplification.

sections.heading: Congruences and proof
sections.text: A congruence compares remainders. We write a ≡ b (mod n) when n divides a − b. Congruences add and multiply: if a ≡ b and c ≡ d (mod n), then a + c ≡ b + d and ac ≡ bd (mod n). Modulo 7, 5 + 6 = 11 ≡ 4, and 3 × 5 = 15 ≡ 1, so 5 is the inverse of 3. The nonzero residues modulo 7 form a multiplicative group; modulo 6 they do not, because 2 × 3 = 6 ≡ 0. Clock arithmetic is the school version. Proof uses definitions and contradiction, for example in proving prime factorisation unique.

keyPoints: A group has an associative operation, an identity and inverses; a field is a commutative ring where every nonzero element has an inverse.
a divides b when b = ak for some integer k, and every integer above 1 has a unique prime factorisation apart from order.
For positive integers a and b, gcd(a, b) × lcm(a, b) = a × b.
a ≡ b (mod n) means n divides a − b; congruences may be added and multiplied.
Modulo a prime p, the nonzero residues form a multiplicative group, so division works as multiplication by an inverse.
Proof in number theory uses definitions, cases and contradiction, and these ideas support school work on factors, fractions and clocks.

en.title: Methods of Teaching Mathematics
en.short: Main mathematics teaching strategies and how to choose and combine them for topics and learners.

sections.heading: Core strategies
sections.text:
A teaching strategy is a planned pattern of teacher and learner activity. Exposition is the teacher explaining a definition, rule or procedure clearly. It is efficient for new content, but learners may stay passive.

Demonstration means showing a worked step while thinking aloud, for example drawing a graph or using a geometry app. Questioning is planned oral checking, from recall to reasoning; allow wait time, a pause of several seconds, after asking. Discussion is structured whole-class talk in which learners compare methods and justify answers. These methods work best together: a short explanation, a demonstration, then questions.

sections.heading: Active strategies
sections.text:
Guided discovery gives learners examples and prompts so they infer a rule, with the teacher correcting and summarising. It builds understanding but needs careful structure. Problem solving asks learners to use unfamiliar tasks and choose a strategy; the teacher models planning, checking and reflection.

Group work means small teams with roles and individual accountability. Projects are extended tasks, such as a class survey, assessed on process and product. All these need clear instructions, time limits and a closing summary.

sections.heading: Choosing and combining
sections.text:
Choose by topic, prior knowledge, class size, resources and the learning aim. New abstract ideas often need exposition and questioning; procedures need demonstration and guided practice; open applications suit problem solving and projects; misconceptions need discussion. No single method suits every lesson.

For example, a teacher in Enugu might teach graph reading in three steps: brief exposition of the axes, demonstration of one example, then pairs solve a new graph and explain their answers. The lesson closes with a whole-class discussion and one exit question. This mix keeps talk precise, gives practice, and checks understanding.

keyPoints: A teaching strategy is a planned pattern of teacher and learner activity, not a single trick.
Exposition explains clearly but should be short and followed by active checking.
Demonstration makes thinking visible by showing and explaining each step.
Guided discovery, problem solving, group work and projects build understanding when well structured and summarised.
Questioning and discussion check reasoning and expose misconceptions.
Choose methods by topic, prior knowledge, resources and learning aim, and combine them in one lesson.

en.title: Assessment and Evaluation in Mathematics
en.short: Formative and summative assessment, validity, item writing, feedback and analysing results.

sections.heading: Purposes and types
sections.text:
Assessment gathers evidence of learning; evaluation judges that evidence against goals. Formative assessment happens during teaching and is used to adjust instruction. Examples include short quizzes, oral questioning and exit tickets.

Summative assessment happens at the end, for example a terminal examination, and usually leads to a grade or certificate. Both matter in mathematics, where errors often reveal misconceptions. A teacher should not use a summative mark as the only feedback.

sections.heading: Validity, reliability, fairness
sections.text:
Validity means the assessment measures what it claims to measure. A test of routine calculation may be invalid as a measure of problem solving. Reliability means consistency: the same scripts marked by different markers, or the same student tested twice, should give similar results.

Fairness means all students have a reasonable chance to show what they know; language, context and access needs must not create unfair barriers. National examination systems and grading rules vary by country, so check the current official syllabus and regulations.

sections.heading: Writing and marking
sections.text:
Write items that match the learning objective. Use clear language and one correct answer for multiple-choice items. Avoid trick questions. Prepare a marking scheme before marking, with method marks for correct reasoning even when the final answer is wrong.

Mark anonymously where possible. Feedback should be specific and timely: say what was wrong and what to do next, not only the score. Give students a chance to act on feedback.

sections.heading: Analysing results
sections.text:
After a test, analyse results. The difficulty index is the proportion who answered an item correctly. If 18 of 30 students answer correctly, difficulty = 18 ÷ 30 = 0.60, or 60 per cent.

The discrimination index compares high and low scorers. If the top third has 8 correct out of 10 and the bottom third has 4 out of 10, discrimination = (8 − 4) ÷ 10 = 0.40. Values near zero suggest the item does not separate stronger from weaker students. Check the mean, range and common wrong answers, then reteach weak topics.

keyPoints: Formative assessment guides teaching; summative assessment grades learning at the end.
Validity is measuring the intended knowledge or skill; reliability is consistency; fairness protects equal opportunity.
Write items from objectives, use a marking scheme with method marks, and give specific feedback.
Difficulty index = number correct ÷ number who attempted the item.
Discrimination index = (high-group correct − low-group correct) ÷ group size.
National examination and grading rules vary by country, so check current official sources.

en.title: Problem Solving and Proof
en.short: Polya’s heuristics, direct proof, contradiction, induction, and classroom reasoning.

sections.heading: Polya’s four steps
sections.text: Problem solving is finding a way when the method is not immediate. A heuristic is a general strategy, not a fixed rule. George Polya described four steps: understand the problem, make a plan, carry out the plan, and look back. In class, ask pupils to restate the task, name what is known and wanted, try a simpler case, draw a diagram, work backwards, or guess and check. A plan may combine several strategies. Looking back means checking the answer, explaining why it works, and asking whether the method transfers. Teachers should allow productive struggle: brief, well-judged hints rather than immediate answers build persistence.

sections.heading: Direct proof and contradiction
sections.text: Proof is a logical argument that a statement is true for all cases. Direct proof starts from definitions and known facts and reaches the conclusion. For example, the sum of two even integers is even: let them be 2m and 2n; then 2m+2n=2(m+n), which is even. Proof by contradiction assumes the statement false and derives an impossibility. To show √2 is irrational, assume √2=a/b in lowest terms; squaring gives a²=2b², so a is even, say a=2c; then 4c²=2b², so b²=2c² and b is even, contradicting lowest terms. Both methods demand precise definitions and clear steps.

sections.heading: Induction and explanation
sections.text: Mathematical induction proves statements about positive integers. It has a base case and an induction step. Claim: 1+3+...+(2n−1)=n². Base: n=1 gives 1=1². Assume true for k: 1+3+...+(2k−1)=k². Adding the next odd number gives k²+(2k+1)=(k+1)², so it holds for k+1. Hence true for all positive integers n. In classrooms, pupils should present proofs in clear sentences, define symbols, and respond to peers. Oral explanation and written proof both develop reasoning and communication. Teachers can model this by thinking aloud and by asking for reasons.

keyPoints: Polya’s four steps are understand the problem, make a plan, carry out the plan, and look back.
A heuristic is a general strategy, not a guaranteed rule.
Direct proof moves from definitions and known facts to the conclusion.
Proof by contradiction assumes the negation and derives an impossibility.
Induction needs a base case and a step from k to k+1; for example 1+3+...+(2n−1)=n².
Pupils build persistence and explanation when teachers give time, model reasoning and ask for reasons.

en.title: Teaching Number and Algebra
en.short: Sequencing number and algebra, representations, misconceptions, models and linking arithmetic to algebra.

sections.heading: Sequencing number
sections.text: School number work usually moves from counting and place value to the four operations, fractions, decimals, ratio and negative numbers. Algebra then extends these ideas to variables, expressions, equations and functions. A common sequence is concrete, pictorial, abstract (CPA): counters, then diagrams, then symbols. It should not be rigid, because older students still need models when an idea is new. Sequencing should revisit earlier ideas and connect them, not treat topics as isolated.

sections.heading: Models and representations
sections.text: A representation is any way of showing a mathematical idea, such as a number line, place-value blocks, a table, a graph or a symbol string. Manipulatives are objects students handle, including counters, base-ten blocks, fraction strips and algebra tiles. They help learners see structure, but the teacher must link the object to the written symbol. Practice builds fluency: short, varied exercises, worked examples and error-analysis tasks are more useful than long repetitive drills alone.

sections.heading: Common misconceptions
sections.text: A misconception is a stable wrong idea that makes sense to the learner, not a careless slip. In number, common errors include ignoring place value, misapplying regrouping, treating the equals sign as “work out the answer”, and adding fractions by adding numerators and denominators. In algebra, students may read 2x as “2 plus x”, combine unlike terms such as 3x + 4, or think a letter always stands for one fixed unknown. Diagnose the reasoning, then use contrasting examples and models to repair it.

sections.heading: Arithmetic to algebra
sections.text: Algebra is generalised arithmetic. Students move from particular calculations to patterns, then express and justify a general rule. For the sequence 4, 7, 10, 13, the common difference is 3, so the nth term is 3n + 1. Check: n = 1 gives 4, n = 2 gives 7. Solving 3n + 1 = 25 gives 3n = 24, so n = 8. The balance model explains why the same operation is applied to both sides.

keyPoints: Number and algebra should be sequenced so that new ideas connect to earlier ones, using concrete, pictorial and abstract representations.
Manipulatives and diagrams help only when the teacher explicitly links them to symbols.
A misconception is a stable wrong idea, so teachers should diagnose reasoning rather than just mark answers wrong.
Common algebra errors include reading 2x as 2 + x and combining unlike terms.
Algebra is generalised arithmetic: patterns are expressed as rules and justified.
For an arithmetic sequence, the nth term is a + (n − 1)d; solve equations by doing the same operation to both sides.

en.title: Teaching Geometry and Measurement
en.short: Teaching shape, space, measurement, geometric reasoning, van Hiele levels, drawing and dynamic geometry.

sections.heading: Geometric thinking
sections.text:
Geometric reasoning develops from recognising shapes to using definitions and proof. The van Hiele model, from Pierre van Hiele and Dina van Hiele-Geldof, describes five levels: visualisation (judging by appearance), analysis (naming properties), informal deduction (ordering properties and simple proofs), formal deduction (proof within a system), and rigour (comparing systems).

Learners may be at different levels for different topics, so teaching should match the level. At visualisation, let students sort shapes; at analysis, ask them to test properties by measuring and folding.

sections.heading: Measurement and units
sections.text:
Measurement connects number and geometry. A measurement has a number and a unit, and the unit must suit the object. Teach length, area, volume, mass, time and angle with concrete instruments: rulers, tapes, balances, clocks and protractors. Unit conversion needs care because area and volume units scale by squares and cubes.

For a rectangle 8 cm by 5 cm, perimeter = 2(8 + 5) = 26 cm and area = 8 × 5 = 40 cm². In metres, 0.08 m × 0.05 m = 0.004 m², which equals 40 cm² because 1 m² = 10,000 cm². Check units.

sections.heading: Drawing and software
sections.text:
Drawing and dynamic geometry make properties visible. Construction with ruler and compass teaches accuracy and the logic of equal radii. Dynamic geometry software such as GeoGebra lets students drag points and watch which properties stay invariant.

A dragged Euclidean triangle keeps its angle sum at 180°; a rectangle keeps right angles only if constructed correctly. Ask students to predict, drag, then explain. This supports visualisation, analysis and deduction.

sections.heading: Difficulties and activities
sections.text:
Common difficulties include confusing perimeter and area, misreading scales, using the wrong unit, and treating a diagram as proof.

Practical activities help: measure the classroom, fold paper to show symmetry and angle sums, build nets of solids, use a geoboard for area, and run a dynamic geometry task on angle properties. Ask for explanations, not only answers.

keyPoints: Geometric reasoning moves through the van Hiele levels from visualisation to rigour.
Match tasks to the learner’s level and move gradually to properties and proof.
Every measurement needs a unit, and area and volume units scale by squares and cubes.
For a rectangle, perimeter = 2(length + width) and area = length × width.
Drawing, construction and dynamic geometry help students see invariant properties.
Common errors include confusing perimeter and area and treating a diagram as proof.

en.title: Teaching Calculus and Analysis
en.short: Teaching limits, derivatives and integrals intuitively, with applications and common misconceptions.

sections.heading: Intuition before formality
sections.text: Begin with change and accumulation, not symbols. A limit is the value a function approaches as the input approaches a point; it need not equal the function value there. Show this with tables and graphs, then with the formal definition. At school level, an intuitive account is appropriate, but the teacher should know the precise definition. Use graphing software to zoom in and ask students to predict.

sections.heading: Derivatives as change
sections.text:
A derivative is the limit of a difference quotient: f′(x) = lim(h→0) [f(x+h) − f(x)] ÷ h. It gives the instantaneous rate of change and the tangent slope. Teach it through secants approaching a tangent, and through speed, cost and growth examples. Worked example: for f(x) = x² at x = 3,
[f(3+h) − f(3)] ÷ h = [(9 + 6h + h²) − 9] ÷ h = 6 + h.
As h tends to 0, the limit is 6. Check by the power rule: f′(x) = 2x, so f′(3) = 6.

sections.heading: Integrals as accumulation
sections.text: A definite integral is the limit of sums of rectangle areas, written as the integral from a to b of f(x) dx. It measures signed accumulation; area below the axis counts negative. Teach Riemann sums with increasing numbers of rectangles, then the fundamental theorem: differentiation and integration are inverse processes, and the integral from a to b of f′(x) dx equals f(b) − f(a). Include applications such as distance from speed, total cost and area between curves. For an indefinite integral, always include the constant of integration, + C.

sections.heading: Misconceptions and rigour
sections.text: Common errors include treating dy/dx as an ordinary fraction, assuming every continuous function is differentiable, and thinking a limit is simply the value at the point. Students may add constants wrongly, ignore units, or find a total by multiplying rate by time when the rate is not constant, instead of integrating. Correct these with counterexamples and graphs. Keep rigour by stating conditions: differentiability implies continuity, but not the converse. Explain when approximations are acceptable and when a proof is needed.

keyPoints: Teach limits through tables, graphs and the formal definition; a limit need not equal the function value.
The derivative is f′(x) = lim(h→0) [f(x+h) − f(x)] ÷ h, the instantaneous rate of change.
Show derivatives as secants approaching a tangent, and check with rules such as f′(x) = 2x for f(x) = x².
A definite integral is a limit of Riemann sums and measures signed accumulation; the integral from a to b of f′(x) dx = f(b) − f(a).
Always include + C for an indefinite integral, and state conditions such as differentiability implying continuity.
Correct misconceptions: dy/dx is not an ordinary fraction, and continuity does not guarantee differentiability.

en.title: Teaching Statistics and Probability
en.short: Teaching data handling, probability, statistical literacy, small projects, graphs, software and misleading claims.

sections.heading: Planning small projects
sections.text: A statistical project follows a cycle: pose a question, plan data collection, collect and clean data, summarise and display, interpret, and report. Define the population (all cases of interest), the sample (cases actually studied) and the variables (characteristics recorded). A biased sample, such as one club only, cannot support a claim about the whole school. Keep projects small and ethical: anonymise responses and seek permission. Check that the question is answerable and the method fits. Privacy rules vary by country; follow local policy.

sections.heading: Data handling and graphs
sections.text: Start with a frequency table: each value or class and its count. The mean is Σx ÷ n, where Σx is the sum of values and n the number of values. For scores 4, 6, 8, 10: mean = 28 ÷ 4 = 7; median = (6 + 8) ÷ 2 = 7; range = 10 − 4 = 6. Choose displays to fit the data: bar charts for categories, histograms for grouped numerical data, box plots for spread, scatterplots for two variables. Teach labels, units and equal class widths. Spreadsheets can sort, tabulate and draw charts, but check formulas and axes.

sections.heading: Probability and simulation
sections.text: Probability is a number from 0 to 1. For equally likely outcomes, P(event) = favourable outcomes ÷ total outcomes. A die gives P(even) = 3 ÷ 6 = 0.5. Relative frequency is the observed proportion in an experiment; it tends to approach theoretical probability as trials increase, but not in a fixed pattern. Simulations make this visible. Address misconceptions such as the gambler’s fallacy: past independent results do not change the next result.

sections.heading: Statistical literacy and errors
sections.text: Statistical literacy is the ability to question and interpret data claims. Ask: Who collected the data? What was the sample? What is missing? Common errors include biased samples, confusing correlation with causation, ignoring base rates (how common something already is), and misleading graphs with truncated axes or unequal intervals. Teach honest redrawing and stated uncertainty. A claim from a small or self-selected sample is limited, not general.

keyPoints: A statistical project moves from question and sampling plan to data collection, cleaning, display, interpretation and report.
Mean = Σx ÷ n; for 4, 6, 8, 10 the mean and median are both 7 and the range is 6.
For equally likely outcomes, P(event) = favourable outcomes ÷ total outcomes; relative frequency approaches probability as trials increase.
Match the display to the data: bar charts for categories, histograms for grouped numerical data, scatterplots for two variables.
Statistical literacy means questioning sample, method, missing data and graph scales before accepting a claim.
Common errors include biased samples, correlation treated as causation, ignored base rates and truncated axes.

en.title: Mathematical Modelling and Applications
en.short: The modelling cycle, worked examples, applications and the limits of models.

sections.heading: The modelling cycle
sections.text: Mathematical modelling begins with a real problem. We make assumptions, which are simplifying choices about what matters and what can be ignored. They produce a mathematical model: an equation, graph, table or algorithm that represents the situation. We solve the model, interpret the solution in real terms, and validate it by comparing with data, checking units, or judging whether the answer is reasonable. If validation fails, we revise the assumptions and repeat. This loop is the modelling cycle.

sections.heading: A worked example
sections.text: An invented business example: a seller has fixed monthly costs of 20,000 naira and makes sachets at 20 naira each, selling at 30 naira. Let n be sachets sold. Profit P = 30n − (20,000 + 20n) = 10n − 20,000. Break-even is P = 0, so n = 2,000. Check: revenue 30 × 2,000 = 60,000; total cost 20,000 + 20 × 2,000 = 60,000; profit 0. It assumes all sachets sell and costs stay fixed.

sections.heading: Science and daily life
sections.text: Science uses models such as exponential growth for populations, but real populations face limits. Daily life uses simple models: travel time is distance ÷ speed, and money left over after shopping is income minus spending. The model keeps only the factors the question needs. When exact data are unavailable, a rough estimate built from sensible guesses is sometimes called a Fermi estimate.

sections.heading: Limits and teaching
sections.text: Models are limited. They depend on assumptions, data quality and the range tested. A population model may ignore migration; a travel-time model ignores traffic. Extrapolation, using a model outside its tested range, is risky. Models can hide value judgements, so users should state assumptions and uncertainty. In teaching, modelling tasks help students see mathematics as useful, but they need clear data, sensible units and time for validation. A model is a tool for thinking, not a final truth.

keyPoints: The modelling cycle is: real problem, assumptions, mathematical model, solution, interpretation and validation, then revision.
Assumptions simplify reality and must be stated, because they shape the model.
For the sachet example, profit is P = 30n − (20,000 + 20n) = 10n − 20,000, and break-even is n = 2,000.
Validate a model by checking units, comparing with data and judging whether the answer is reasonable.
Models have limits: they depend on data and assumptions, and extrapolation can mislead.
In teaching, modelling tasks need clear data, sensible units and time for interpretation and validation.

en.title: Educational Technology in Mathematics
en.short: Choosing and integrating calculators, spreadsheets, geometry and algebra software, LMS and online resources.

sections.heading: Tools and roles
sections.text: Calculators handle arithmetic and functions quickly, freeing lesson time for estimation and interpretation. Spreadsheets organise data in rows and columns and recalculate formulas automatically. Dynamic geometry software lets students drag points and see which properties stay true, so a theorem becomes a pattern to test. Computer algebra systems (CAS) manipulate symbols exactly, for example expanding (x + 2)² or solving equations. Each tool changes what is easy to teach: a graph can be explored in seconds, but students still need to explain why the result is true.

sections.heading: Selection and integration
sections.text: Choose a tool by matching it to the learning objective, not by novelty. Check cost and licence, device and browser needs, language, accessibility, data privacy, and whether it works offline. Integrate it into a planned task with a clear purpose. In a spreadsheet lesson on mean, enter scores 60, 70, 80 and 90 in cells A1 to A4. The formula =AVERAGE(A1:A4) returns 75, because (60 + 70 + 80 + 90) ÷ 4 = 300 ÷ 4 = 75. Ask students to change one score and predict the new mean before recalculating.

sections.heading: Access and limits
sections.text: A learning management system (LMS) such as Moodle or Google Classroom stores notes, quizzes and submissions, and can give feedback. Online resources include videos, simulations and open textbooks; check the author, date and accuracy before use. Access is uneven. Electricity, data cost, shared devices and weak networks can exclude students, so provide printable alternatives and avoid requiring one private device. Technology can distract, encourage button-pressing without reasoning, or hide errors through rounded displays. Teachers should test the task beforehand, set rules for use, and keep paper methods visible. Local school policy and examination rules on calculators vary by country, so check the current official regulations.

keyPoints: Match each digital tool to a clear learning objective and check cost, access and privacy.
Calculators and spreadsheets speed calculation, but students must still estimate and interpret answers.
Dynamic geometry supports conjecture and proof by letting students drag and test properties.
Computer algebra systems manipulate symbols, so lessons must require explanation, not only answers.
An LMS organises resources and feedback, but offline alternatives are needed where access is limited.
In the spreadsheet example, =AVERAGE(A1:A4) gives 75 for 60, 70, 80 and 90, since 300 ÷ 4 = 75.

en.title: Inclusive and Differentiated Mathematics
en.short: Planning mixed-ability maths lessons, support for disabilities and gifted learners, UDL and fair assessment.

sections.heading: Planning for mixed ability
sections.text: Inclusive mathematics teaching starts with a clear learning goal that most learners can reach, then plans several routes to it. Differentiation means adapting content, process, product or environment so each learner works at an appropriate level without losing the main idea. Universal design for learning (UDL) goes further: it builds options into the lesson from the start through multiple means of engagement, representation, and action and expression. A teacher might present a fraction idea with objects, diagrams and symbols, then let learners explain in speech, writing or drawing.

sections.heading: Support and challenge
sections.text: Learners with disabilities or mathematics difficulties need scaffolds: worked examples, concrete materials, step-by-step prompts, extra time, large print or assistive technology. Use the learner’s strengths and check the fit of supports. Do not confuse support with lowering expectations. Gifted learners need enrichment or acceleration: open problems, proof tasks, independent projects, or faster progression. A small case: in a mixed class, a teacher gives all learners the same problem on sharing 24 mangoes among 6 baskets, then offers counters to some, a table to others, and an extension asking for a general rule for n baskets. All work on the same concept.

sections.heading: Fair assessment
sections.text: Fair assessment judges the mathematics, not the disability or the language. State criteria clearly, use varied formats, and give approved accommodations such as extra time or a reader without changing the learning standard. Separate effort and behaviour from mathematical accuracy. Use short diagnostic checks to adjust grouping and support. Report progress against goals, and involve learners and, where appropriate, parents or guardians.

sections.heading: Working with others
sections.text: Inclusion is a shared responsibility. Plan with support teachers, special educators and families, and follow national policy and school guidance, which differ by country. Review what worked after each lesson. The aim is not a separate curriculum for each learner but a classroom where all learners can take part in worthwhile mathematics.

keyPoints: Inclusive planning starts from a clear goal and builds several routes to it.
Differentiation adapts content, process, product or environment; UDL builds options in from the start.
Scaffolds such as worked examples, concrete materials and assistive technology support learners without lowering the core goal.
Gifted learners need enrichment or acceleration, not just more of the same work.
Fair assessment judges mathematics with clear criteria and approved accommodations.
Inclusion is shared with colleagues and families, and policy varies by country.

en.title: Language and Communication in Mathematics
en.short: Mathematical language, word problems, classroom talk and multilingual code-switching.

sections.heading: Mathematical language
sections.text: Mathematics has its own register: the words, symbols and grammar used to express mathematical ideas. Definitions must be exact. A prime number, for example, is a whole number greater than 1 with exactly two positive divisors. The phrase 'divisible only by 1 and itself' wrongly includes 1. Symbols such as = and × are conventions; learners need to read them aloud and translate between words and symbols. Everyday words like 'product' and 'difference' carry special meanings in mathematics, so teach them explicitly.

sections.heading: Reading word problems
sections.text: Word problems mix everyday language with mathematical structure. Difficulties often come from vocabulary, long sentences, implied information and unfamiliar contexts. Teach learners to read aloud, restate in their own words, list what is known and unknown, and draw a diagram. Example: 'Ada is 3 years older than twice Chidi’s age. Ada is 15. How old is Chidi?' Let Chidi’s age be c. Then 2c + 3 = 15, so 2c = 12 and c = 6. Check: 2 × 6 + 3 = 15. The order of the words matters.

sections.heading: Classroom discourse
sections.text: Classroom discourse is the talk through which mathematics is taught and learned. Learners should explain reasoning, not only give answers. Useful teacher moves include waiting after a question, revoicing a learner’s idea ('So you are saying that...'), and asking 'why?' or 'can someone add to that?'. Encourage full sentences and precise terms. Pair work gives quieter learners time to rehearse an explanation.

sections.heading: Multilingual settings
sections.text: In multilingual classrooms, code-switching means alternating between languages during a lesson. It can be a resource: a learner may understand a new idea in a familiar language, then bridge to the language of instruction and to mathematical terms. Allow brief explanation in the home language, then ask for a summary in the official language. Language-of-instruction policy differs by country and school, so check your current national policy. The aim is confident use of mathematical language in the language of assessment.

keyPoints: Mathematical register is the specialised vocabulary, symbols and grammar of mathematics, and definitions must be exact.
Everyday words such as product and difference have different meanings in mathematics.
Reading a word problem means restating it, listing knowns and unknowns, and noting that the order of the words changes the meaning.
Classroom discourse should require learners to explain reasoning, using wait time and revoicing.
Code-switching can support understanding, but learners must also master the language of instruction and assessment.
Language-of-instruction policy varies by country and school, so check the current official policy.

en.title: Teacher Professionalism and Ethics
en.short: Professional role, ethical duties, fairness, confidentiality, child protection and academic integrity.

sections.heading: Professional role
sections.text:
A profession rests on specialised knowledge, standards and accountability. A teacher’s role includes planning and teaching mathematics, assessing fairly, pastoral care, working with parents and colleagues, and keeping professional boundaries. Professionalism means competence, punctuality, reflection and respect for learners.

Registration bodies and codes are country-specific. Examples include the Teachers Registration Council of Nigeria (TRCN), Ghana’s National Teaching Council, Kenya’s Teachers Service Commission and England’s Teaching Regulation Agency. Rules change, so check the current official version. Legal duties usually include duty of care (taking reasonable steps to keep learners safe from foreseeable harm), health and safety, data protection and education law.

sections.heading: Ethics and fairness
sections.text:
Ethics are principles that guide right action. Fairness means treating learners equitably, avoiding discrimination, applying marking criteria consistently and managing conflicts of interest. A teacher should not accept gifts that could influence grades.

Case: Mrs Adeyemi, a mathematics teacher in Lagos, is offered money by a parent to raise a test mark. She declines, records the approach and asks a colleague to moderate borderline scripts. This protects trust and fair assessment.

sections.heading: Confidentiality and protection
sections.text:
Confidentiality means keeping learner information private. Share it only with staff who need to know, with parents as appropriate, or when safeguarding or the law requires disclosure. Do not discuss named learners publicly or on social media.

Child protection, also called safeguarding, is the duty to keep children safe. Teachers should recognise possible signs of harm, record facts and report concerns promptly to the school’s designated officer or the relevant authority. Do not investigate alone. Follow local procedures and avoid unobserved private contact.

sections.heading: Integrity and law
sections.text:
Academic integrity means honesty in teaching, assessment and research. Set clear rules on plagiarism, exam conduct and citation, and do not falsify records or help cheating. Teachers should model the standards they expect.

Legal duties include duty of care, health and safety, data protection, copyright and reporting obligations. These duties differ by country and school and change. Check the current teacher code, school policy and national law before acting.

keyPoints: Professionalism combines subject knowledge, teaching skill, accountability and ethical conduct.
Teacher registration bodies and codes are country-specific; check the current official rules.
Fairness means consistent marking, no discrimination and managing conflicts of interest.
Keep learner information confidential and share it only on a need-to-know or legal basis.
Child protection requires recognising concerns, recording facts and reporting promptly under local procedures.
Academic integrity requires honest assessment, clear rules and modelling the standards expected.

en.title: Teaching Practice and Reflective Practice
en.short: School observation, microteaching, supervised practice, mentor feedback, reflective journals and portfolios.

sections.heading: Observation and microteaching
sections.text: School observation means watching an experienced teacher’s mathematics lessons and noting how the lesson is planned, how pupils are managed and how explanations and questions are used. Observe one focus at a time, such as transitions or board work, and record evidence, not judgements. Microteaching is a short lesson taught to peers or a small group and followed by feedback. It lets you practise one skill, such as asking clear questions, in a low-risk setting. Check your institution’s rules for lesson length.

sections.heading: Supervised teaching practice
sections.text: Supervised teaching practice is a block of real school teaching, observed and assessed by a school mentor and a university or college supervisor. Plan each lesson with clear objectives, a starter, sequenced activities and a plenary. Classroom management means setting routines, using names, moving around the room and correcting low-level disruption early. For example, Amaka, a B.Ed student in Nigeria, writes her plan, checks the examples, and agrees with her mentor that she will call on quieter pupils. She keeps the mentor’s written feedback with the lesson plan.

sections.heading: Reflection and portfolios
sections.text: A reflective journal is a regular written record of what happened, why it happened and what you will change. Use a simple cycle: describe, analyse, plan. Avoid blaming pupils; focus on your decisions. A professional portfolio is a curated collection of evidence, such as lesson plans, mentor reports, samples of pupils’ work and your reflections. It shows growth over time and supports job applications. Remove pupils’ names or follow your school’s confidentiality rules.

sections.heading: Feedback and self-evaluation
sections.text: Mentor feedback should be specific and tied to evidence. Ask for one strength and one priority. Self-evaluation means judging your lesson against its objectives and your own targets, not against your feelings. After a lesson, ask: did pupils meet the objective, where did time go, and what will I do differently? Record the answer and act on it in the next lesson. Requirements for teaching practice vary by country and institution, so check the current handbook.

keyPoints: School observation should record evidence against a focus, not personal judgements.
Microteaching lets you practise one teaching skill in a short, low-risk lesson.
Supervised teaching practice is assessed by a school mentor and an institutional supervisor.
Plan lessons with clear objectives and manage routines early.
Reflective journals use describe, analyse and plan to turn experience into learning.
Portfolios collect evidence of growth, and teaching practice rules vary by country and institution.

en.title: Research Methods in Mathematics Education
en.short: Designs, sampling, instruments, ethics and simple analysis for small mathematics education studies.

sections.heading: Designs and questions
sections.text: Research starts with a clear question. Quantitative designs test measurable relationships, often by survey or quasi-experiment. A quasi-experiment compares groups without random assignment, which is common in schools. Qualitative designs explore meaning, for example through case study, interviews or classroom observation. Mixed methods combine both. Action research is a small cycle: plan, act, observe, reflect, often used by a teacher to improve their own practice. A final-year project usually follows the same logic on a larger scale.

sections.heading: Data and sampling
sections.text: Quantitative data are numbers, such as test scores or counts. Qualitative data are words, images or observations. The population is everyone you want to describe; the sample is the group you actually study. Random sampling gives each member a known chance of selection and reduces bias. Convenience sampling uses whoever is available and limits generalisation. Define each variable, which is any characteristic that can take different values, and state how you will measure it.

sections.heading: Instruments and ethics
sections.text: Instruments include questionnaires, interviews, observation schedules and tests. A questionnaire must be clear and pilot-tested. Validity means the instrument measures what it claims; reliability means it gives consistent results. Triangulation uses more than one source or method to strengthen a claim. Ethics require informed consent, voluntary participation, confidentiality, anonymity where promised, and care with children. In most institutions you need approval from a research ethics committee before collecting data; rules vary by country and institution, so check yours.

sections.heading: Simple analysis
sections.text: Counts and percentages summarise categorical data, which are data that fall into groups such as yes or no answers. For example, if 24 of 40 students say they enjoy mathematics, the percentage is 24 ÷ 40 × 100 = 60%. For numerical data, the mean is the sum divided by the number of values: for 40, 50, 60, 70 and 80, the mean is 300 ÷ 5 = 60. Qualitative data are coded into themes. Report limitations and do not claim causation from correlation alone.

keyPoints: A clear research question decides whether a quantitative, qualitative, mixed methods or action research design fits.
The population is the whole group of interest; the sample is the part studied, and random sampling reduces bias.
Validity is about measuring the right thing; reliability is about getting consistent results.
Ethics approval, informed consent and confidentiality are needed before data collection; check your institution and country rules.
Percentages are part ÷ total × 100; the mean is the sum of values ÷ number of values.
